# Background
Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a group of genetic disorders in which red blood cells contort into a sickle shape. Symptoms of SCD include anemia (caused by misshapen cells dying early) as well as pain, infection, and stroke (caused by sickle cells blocking blood flow). There is some evidence that exposure to air pollution aggravates vaso-occlusion and pain in SCD patients.

A hematologist at Duke wants to study the associations between various air pollutants and SCD in Durham County, North Carolina. She provides data on health system utilization (i.e., emergency department visits, hospitalizations, etc.) for SCD and you obtain air pollution data from the EPA. The pollutant data are raw measurements taken from the air pollution monitor at the RDU airport. This exposure data is messy and will need to be processed. You will write a function to process your data and do some exploratory data analysis (EDA) using tables and plots.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
# Function

# Order of things in function:
# Rename columns with more appropriate variable names
# Remove duplicate rows
# Negative values - set to 0
# Calculate daily average (if more than one value)
# Format date correctly
# Argument for ppb ppm conversion
# Return results as a tibble/data frame with a single row per day

organizer <- function(file,
                      O3_units) {

  # Read the .csv file (data file)
  data <- read.csv(file,
                   header = TRUE)

  # Rename columns
  data <- data %>%
  
    rename(CO_ppm = Daily.Max.8.hour.CO.Concentration,
           PM2.5_ug_m3_LC = Daily.Mean.PM2.5.Concentration,
           O3_ppm = Daily.Max.8.hour.Ozone.Concentration)
    
  # Remove duplicate rows (rows that are EXACTLY the same)
  data <- distinct(data)
  
  # Set any negative values to 0
  for (i in 1:ncol(data)) {
  
    data[, i][data[, i] < 0] <- 0
  
  }

  # Calculate average for those that have more than one value
  data <- data %>%
  
    group_by(Date) %>%
  
    summarize(CO_ppm = mean(CO_ppm),
              PM2.5_ug_m3_LC = mean(PM2.5_ug_m3_LC),
              O3_ppm = mean(O3_ppm))

  # Format date
  data <- data %>%
  
    mutate(Date = mdy(Date)) %>%
  
    arrange(Date)

  # ppb ppm conversion
  if (O3_units == "ppb") {
  
    data <- data %>%

      mutate(O3_ppm = O3_ppm * 1000,
             CO_ppm = CO_ppm * 1000) %>%

      rename(CO_ppb = CO_ppm,
             O3_ppb = O3_ppm)

  }

  return(data)

}

```

**Think carefully about the order in which your function does these steps. Does the order change your results?**

Yes, the order can change the results as some steps can influence subsequent calculations. For example, performing the average calculations before removing negative and duplicate values would result in incorrect averages. Converting the date format before grouping is also better as it ensures the observations corresponding to the same date are grouped together even if the formats are different. 

```{r, echo=FALSE, results='hide'}
# Merge into one dataset

# Dataset where units are in ppm
data2018 <- organizer("AQ_2018.csv",
                      "ppm")

data2019 <- organizer("AQ_2019.csv",
                      "ppm")

data2020 <- organizer("AQ_2020.csv",
                      "ppm")

df_ppm <- bind_rows(data2018,
                    data2019,
                    data2020)
df_ppm
```

## Tables

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Function for table (checks what units it is and generates it with those labels)
table <- function(data) {
  
  col_names <- names(data)
  
  ppb <- any(grepl("ppb", 
                   col_names,
                   ignore.case = TRUE))

  ppm <- any(grepl("ppm",
                   col_names,
                   ignore.case = TRUE))

  if (ppb) {
    
    # Generates the ppb table
    
    # Creates the dataset for the table by grouping them by year
    # It then calculates the minimums and maximums
    data <- data %>%

      mutate(Year = as.character(year(Date))) %>%
 
      group_by(Year) %>%
 
      summarize(across(c(CO_ppb, 
                         PM2.5_ug_m3_LC, 
                         O3_ppb),
                       list(Min = ~ format(round(min(.x, 
                                                     na.rm = TRUE), 
                                                 3),
                                           nsmall = 3),
                            Max = ~ format(round(max(.x, 
                                                     na.rm = TRUE),
                                                 3),
                                           nsmall = 3))))

    # Creating the table from the data 
    table <- flextable(data) %>%
      
      # Aesthetics (labels, titles, alignment of the table)
      set_header_labels(Year = "Year",
                        CO_ppb_Min = "Minimum CO Concentration (ppb)",
                        CO_ppb_Max = "Maximum CO Concentration (ppb)",
                        PM2.5_ug_m3_LC_Min = "Minimum PM2.5 Concentration (µg/m³ LC)",
                        PM2.5_ug_m3_LC_Max = "Maximum PM2.5 Concentration (µg/m³ LC)",
                        O3_ppb_Min = "Minimum O3 (Ozone) Concentration (ppb)",
                        O3_ppb_Max = "Maximum O3 (Ozone) Concentration (ppb)") %>%

      set_header_labels(values = paste("Maximum (Max.) and Minimum (Min.) Pollutant Concentrations (Conc.) for ",
                                       unique(data$Year))) %>%

      theme_booktabs() %>%

      bold(part = "header") %>%

      flextable::align(align = "center",
            part = "all") %>%

      autofit() %>%

      set_table_properties(layout = "autofit",
                           width = 1,
                           align = "center")

  } else {
    
    # If the units are not ppb, then they should be ppm
    # This part is the exact same as the ppb aspect earlier. Only the units differ
     data <- data %>%

       mutate(Year = as.character(year(Date))) %>%

       group_by(Year) %>%

       summarize(across(c(CO_ppm, 
                          PM2.5_ug_m3_LC, 
                          O3_ppm),
                        list(Min = ~ format(round(min(.x, 
                                                      na.rm = TRUE), 
                                                  3),
                                            nsmall = 3),
                             Max = ~ format(round(max(.x, 
                                                      na.rm = TRUE),
                                                  3),
                                            nsmall = 3)))) 

    # Creating the table from the data
    table <- flextable(data) %>%

      # Aesthetics (labels, titles, alignment of the table)
      set_header_labels(Year = "Year",
                        CO_ppm_Min = "Min. CO Conc. (ppm)",
                        CO_ppm_Max = "Maximum CO Conc. (ppm)",
                        PM2.5_ug_m3_LC_Min = "Min. PM2.5 Conc. (µg/m³ LC)",
                        PM2.5_ug_m3_LC_Max = "Max. PM2.5 Conc. (µg/m³ LC)",
                        O3_ppm_Min = "Min. O3 (Ozone) Conc. (ppm)",
                        O3_ppm_Max = "Max. O3 (Ozone) Conc. (ppm)") %>%

      add_header_lines(values = paste("Maximum (Max.) and Minimum (Min.) Pollutant Concentrations (Conc.) for",
                                      unique(data$Year))) %>% 

      theme_booktabs() %>%

      bold(part = "header") %>%

      flextable::align(align = "center",
            part = "all") %>%

      autofit() %>%

      set_table_properties(layout = "autofit",
                           width = 1,
                           align = "center")

  }
  
  # Return table so it prints after function is complete
  return(table)

}

```

## Plot 1: CO and O3 by month.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Create the data frame for the plot
plot1df <- df_ppm %>%
  
  # Reformat the date (only the month is kept)
  mutate(Date = format(Date,
                       "%b")) %>%
  
  # Group them by date
  group_by(Date) %>%

  # Perform summary calculations (mean, standard deviation)
  # Also counts how many values there are in a specific month
  summarize(CO_count = sum(!is.na(CO_ppm)),
            CO_ppm_sd = sd(CO_ppm,
                           na.rm = TRUE),
            CO_ppm = mean(CO_ppm,
                          na.rm = TRUE),
            
            O3_count = sum(!is.na(O3_ppm)),
            O3_ppm_sd = sd(O3_ppm,
                           na.rm = TRUE),
            O3_ppm = mean(O3_ppm,
                          na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") %>%

  # Change format from wide to long (easier for creating the plot)
  pivot_longer(cols = c(CO_ppm, O3_ppm),
               names_to = "Pollutant",
               values_to = "Concentration") %>%
  
  # Determining which SD and count should be used to calculate the confidence intervals
  mutate(SD = ifelse(Pollutant == "CO_ppm",
                     CO_ppm_sd,
                     O3_ppm_sd),
         Count = ifelse(Pollutant == "CO_ppm",
                        CO_count,
                        O3_count))

```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Graphing Plot 1
ggplot(data = plot1df,
       aes(x = Date,
           y = Concentration,
           color = Pollutant,
           group = Pollutant)) +

  # Plot the data (a lined scatterplot)
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +

  geom_point(size = 2) +

  # Plot the confidence intervals
  geom_errorbar(aes(x = Date,
                     ymin = Concentration - 1.96 * SD/sqrt(Count),
                     ymax = Concentration + 1.96 * SD/sqrt(Count)),
                 width = 0.2) +
  
  # Set the colors of the pollutant data as well as their labels
  scale_color_manual(values = c("CO_ppm" = "purple",
                               "O3_ppm" = "blue"),
                     labels = c("CO_ppm" = "Carbon Monoxide (CO)",
                                "O3_ppm" = "Ozone (O3)")) +

  # Aesthetics, limits, and axes/title labels for the plot
  theme_minimal() + 

  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.line = element_line(color = "black"),
        legend.position = "top",
        legend.direction = "horizontal") + 

  scale_x_discrete(limits = month.abb,
                   guide = guide_axis(angle = 45)) +

  facet_wrap(~ Pollutant,
             scales = "free_y",
             ncol = 1,
             labeller = as_labeller(c("CO_ppm" = " ",
                                      "O3_ppm" = " "))) + 

  labs(title = "Pollutant (O3 and CO) Measurements by Month",
       x = "Month",
       y = "Concentration (ppm)",
       color = "")

```

Note: Because the 2020 data stops in April, the averages for January-April are based on three years of data, while May-December are only based on two.

The concentrations for CO and O3, while in the same units, are on very different scales, so the two variables were graphed separately before being combined them into a single image. With this method, both of their scales were accounted for while allowing their graphs to be viewed side-by-side to visually see their differences.

## Plot 2: PM2.5 by month and year.

Month on the x-axis and PM2.5 concentration on the y-axis. Include year as different colors. Use whatever geom you think best displays the data. There is no “correct” geom, but some are better than others. Consider readability - what conveys any patterns in your data best? Below the plot, write a 1-sentence justification of your choice of geom.
```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Create the data frame for Plot 2
plot2df <- df_ppm %>%

  # Change the date to month and year
  mutate(Year = year(Date),
         Month = month(Date,
                       label = TRUE,
                       abbr = TRUE)) %>%

  # Group the data by month and year
  group_by(Year, Month) %>%
  
  # Calculate the averages of PM2.5
  summarize(PM2.5_ug_m3_LC = mean(PM2.5_ug_m3_LC,
                                  na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")

```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Graphing Plot 2
ggplot(data = plot2df,
       aes(x = Month,
           y = PM2.5_ug_m3_LC,
           color = factor(Year),
           group = Year)) +

  # Plot lines for the three years (connecting the points)
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  
  # Plot the values for the three years (points)
  geom_point(size = 1) +

  # Graph customization (theme, colors for the years, and labels)
  theme_minimal() + 

  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.line = element_line(color = "black")) +

  scale_color_manual(values = c("2018" = "blue",
                                "2019" = "darkgreen",
                                "2020" = "purple")) +

  labs(title = "PM2.5 Measurements by Month and Year",
       x = "Month",
       y = "PM 2.5 (ug/m3 LC)",
       color = "Year")

```

I chose to graph it with a connected scatterplot as I felt it was a good way to show how the concentrations of PM2.5 change over time. 

## Interpretation 
**In 2-3 sentences, describe the patterns you see in your tables and plots. For example: Do any pollutants show seasonal patterns? Do any years stand out? Keep in mind which months have less data.**

Plot 1 suggests that ozone concentrations increase during the warmer seasons (spring and summer) compared to the colder months, while carbon monoxide concentrations see the opposite trend (increase in the colder months, and decrease in the warmer ones). Plot 2 suggests that the changes in PM2.5 concentration is more varied, though sharp increases are seen in the colder months (as shown for all three years) as well as in the summer (as seen in 2018 and 2019). As a result, Plot 1 indicates that ozone and carbon monoxide show a seasonal pattern, while PM2.5 shows a more complex and varied one.

## AI Use Statement
I used AI to help me with the grepl() function, which detects whether the units for carbon monoxide (CO) and O3 (ozone) are in ppb or ppm by reading through the names of the columns in the dataset. I also used it to help me with setting the table properties and formatting the table so it appears better in the knitted word document. This also includes changing the dataset in the function so it shows the minimum and maximum values rounded to three decimal places; I thought it would be better to do it all in one instead of separately. I used AI to help me format certain aspects of the graphs, such as tilting the labels on the x-axis to make them readable (for the second plot) and also making sure that the months were in order (for the first plot), as they for some reason were coming out as alphabetical instead. I also used it to understand the facet_wrap() and pivot_longer() functions better (for the first plot), and I also used it to double check what I wanted to do for the confidence intervals. There were times in which I wrote the code but was unable to get it to run. In those instances, if other sources (such as Stack Overflow) were not helpful, I would use AI to help me troubleshoot and fix the error(s). I also used AI to double check my thinking for some of the questions.
